opus-5.5.text:
I think part of it is a matter of where you look and at what timescale. A lot of the constructivist tradition in the history and sociology of technology, think of the social construction of technology school, built its case through really careful, close-up case studies: the bicycle, the fluorescent lamp, Bakelite, particular missile guidance systems. When you zoom in that closely on a single artifact in a single society over a decade or two, you do see enormous contingency. You see relevant social groups fighting over what the technology means, interpretive flexibility, design choices that could easily have gone another way. And that's real; I don't want to dismiss it.

But the selection pressures from military and economic competition operate at a different level. They act on whole societies over longer periods. They're often invisible in any given case study because they work through the background conditions: which states survive, which firms stay solvent, which practices get copied because the people who didn't adopt them lost. If you're studying how engineers and users negotiated the design of something, you won't necessarily see the counterfactual society that made a different choice and was outcompeted, because that society is often not around to be studied, or it's a footnote. There's a survivorship bias built into the archive.

There's also, I think, an intellectual and somewhat normative motivation. Constructivism arose partly as a reaction against crude technological determinism, the idea that technology marches forward on its own logic and society just adapts. Scholars were rightly keen to restore human agency, to say these outcomes are choices, they're political, they could be otherwise. That's an important corrective. But in the course of pushing back, there's a tendency to treat any talk of structural pressure as if it were the naive determinism being rejected. And so the more sophisticated version, which I'd call something like a competitive or evolutionary account, gets lumped in and dismissed.

What I'd argue is that you can hold both. Locally, in the short run, there's a great deal of contingency and social shaping. But at the macro level, when there's intense military-economic competition between groups, technologies that confer power tend to get adopted and spread, regardless of whether any particular group wanted them, because the alternative is falling behind or being displaced. Think of how the military revolution in early modern Europe forced fiscal and administrative changes on states, or how industrialization spread after the Opium Wars and the Meiji period. Japan's leaders didn't adopt industrial and military technology because of some local negotiation of meaning; they did it because they saw what happened to China.

And this matters a lot for thinking about AI. If you only take the constructivist lens, you might conclude that we can simply decide, as a society, what kind of AI we want, and that's the end of it. I think we do have real agency, but that agency is constrained by competitive dynamics between firms and between states. If we want to steer the technology, we have to take those pressures seriously, and often that means working on the competitive structure itself: coordination, agreements, governance that shifts the incentives, rather than assuming good intentions in any one lab or country will be enough.

r001.rationale: It says close-up case studies reveal local contingency while making broader competitive selection pressures less visible.

r002.rationale: It directly contrasts close-up studies of single artifacts over decades with competition acting on whole societies over longer periods.

r003.rationale: It describes structural pressures and gives an example of Japanese leaders reacting to China, but does not clearly state that much of competition’s influence works through people internalizing its threat.

r004.rationale: It says constructivists may mistake structural pressure for rejected technological determinism, but does not identify ambiguity between internalized competitive pressure and ideology.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to the level of analysis they're working at. Constructivist historians, and the social construction of technology tradition more broadly, have done really valuable work showing that at the micro level, the trajectory of a given technology is heavily shaped by contingent factors: the particular engineers involved, the cultural meanings attached to the artifact, the interest groups that happened to win out, the political context. And when you look closely at any individual case, those contingencies are everywhere. The bicycle could have taken many forms; the layout of a particular factory reflected labor politics as much as engineering logic. So the natural conclusion from that body of work is that technology isn't determined by some internal logic, and that society has a lot of latitude in shaping it.

But the problem is that those studies tend to look at individual cases, within a single society, over a relatively short time horizon. And at that scale you don't see the selection pressure operating. Military and economic competition act more like an evolutionary filter that operates across societies and over longer periods. Any single actor might choose to forgo a technology, or shape it in some idiosyncratic direction, but if that choice makes them less competitive, they lose relative power, they lose market share, they get conquered or absorbed or imitated. And the actors who did adopt the more effective technology, or the more effective way of organizing around it, are the ones who persist and get copied.

So you can have a world where every individual choice is genuinely contingent and socially constructed, and yet the aggregate outcome looks quite deterministic, because competition is weeding out the choices that don't work. The historian looking at one case sees freedom; the person looking at the system sees convergence. Both are right about what they're seeing, but if you only do the micro-level work, you'll systematically underestimate how much the structural pressures constrain where things end up.

I'd add that there's also something about disciplinary temperament. A lot of the constructivist turn was a reaction against crude technological determinism, and against triumphalist narratives about progress. That was a healthy correction. But it means there's a kind of professional incentive to emphasize contingency and agency and to be suspicious of anything that smells like structure or inevitability. Military competition in particular is an uncomfortable topic, because it suggests that even if everyone would prefer not to develop some capability, they may feel compelled to anyway. That's a grim story, and I think there's a reluctance to foreground it.

Which matters a great deal for how we think about AI, because if you believe the constructivist picture is the whole story, you'll think the main challenge is getting the right values into the right rooms. If you take the competitive pressures seriously, you realize that even well-intentioned actors can be pushed toward outcomes nobody wants, and that the governance problem is partly about changing the structure of the competition itself.

r001.rationale: The response says case-focused research highlights contingency while missing structural selection pressures that operate across societies and longer periods.

r002.rationale: It directly contrasts individual cases at the micro level with competition acting across societies over longer time horizons.

r003.rationale: The response describes actors being pressured by competition, but does not say that its influence operates through people internalising its threat.

r004.rationale: It does not identify ambiguity between explaining behaviour through internalised competition and explaining it through ideology.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is a reaction against technological determinism: the idea that technology develops according to its own logic and then determines what society looks like. Constructivist historians have done valuable work showing that particular technologies reflect choices, interests, and contingent circumstances. Things could have developed differently.

But that doesn’t mean all those possibilities are equally sustainable under competition. A society can choose not to adopt a technology, or to develop it in a particular way, but those choices may affect its ability to compete economically or militarily. Over time, that can put quite strong constraints on which arrangements survive and spread.

So there are two different questions: why did these people make this particular choice, and why do we see some kinds of choices becoming prevalent across societies over long periods? If you focus on the first, you can demonstrate a lot of contingency while missing the selection pressures operating at the second level. You don’t need to think technology has an inevitable trajectory to think those pressures give technological development a direction.

r001.rationale: The response says focusing on individual choices can miss selection pressures, but does not attribute that oversight to a bias toward what preferred research methods reveal.

r002.rationale: It contrasts particular choices with patterns across societies over time, but does not explain that competition is less visible at the microhistorical scale than at the macrohistorical scale.

r003.rationale: The response discusses competitive constraints and selection pressures, but not the influence of people internalising the threat of competition.

r004.rationale: The response does not identify ambiguity between explaining behavior through internalised competition and explaining it through ideology.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is a reaction against a very simplistic technological determinism—the idea that technologies arrive according to some internal logic, and then society just adapts to them. The constructivists rightly point out that people make choices about what gets developed, that interests and institutions matter, and that things could have gone differently.

But showing that there are choices doesn’t establish that those choices are unconstrained. If you focus on a particular invention or a particular society, you can see all this contingency. What’s harder to see at that scale is the selection pressure operating across societies over a longer period. A state can choose not to adopt a technology, but if that puts it at a substantial military or economic disadvantage, it may lose influence, be conquered, or eventually feel compelled to adopt it.

So social construction and competitive pressure can both be real. There can be many possible paths locally, while competition systematically favours some paths over others. My concern is that, in correcting the overly deterministic story, we can lose sight of that broader constraint.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a reaction against technological determinism and the limits of focusing on one invention or society, but does not attribute the oversight to bias toward preferred research methods.

r002.rationale: It says competitive selection pressure is harder to see when examining a particular invention or society than across societies over a longer period.

r003.rationale: It says states may feel compelled to adopt technologies under competitive pressure, but does not explain that the influence operates through people internalising the threat.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss ambiguity between internalised competition and ideology.
